title: Cleft sentences
tagline: Split one sentence into two so the listener knows exactly which part matters.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (IT, WHAT, ALL, REASON)
Writing Part 1 — essay: emphasis and correction
Speaking Parts 3 and 4 — highlighting the point you most want to make
Listening — recognising emphasis in spoken argument
why: Cleft sentences let a writer or speaker point at exactly one piece of information — this fact, not that one — instead of leaving the reader to guess. C1 Advanced rewards this precision in the essay, and Part 4 regularly hides an it-cleft or wh-cleft behind an ordinary-looking key word.

diagrams.title: Splitting a sentence for emphasis

before.text: The message mattered, not the delivery.

after.text: It was the message that mattered, not the delivery.

steps: Put It + a form of be at the front.
Add the element you want to focus on straight after: the message.
Follow it with that (or who / which) and the rest of the original sentence.

rows.label: Example
cells: It was Nadia who found the mistake.

rows.label: Typical use
cells: Building up to an action, need or feeling

head: Pattern
Structure
Example
rows: It was the last question that caught everyone out.
It was Liam who spotted the error first.
It + be + not + noun phrase + but …
It wasn't the exam that worried her, but the interview afterwards.
What surprised the teacher was the level of detail.
All she wanted was a straight answer.
The reason the trip was cancelled was the weather.
The only thing + clause + be + focus
The only thing that matters now is the final result.

use.point: it-clefts: singling out one fact for emphasis or correction

examples.text: It was Sofia's presentation that convinced the judges, not the data itself.
It wasn't the distance that put them off, but the cost of the flights.
It is precisely this kind of detail that separates a good essay from an excellent one.

use.point: wh-clefts: building up to the important information

examples.text: What worries me is the lack of preparation, not the difficulty of the exam.
examples.note: the focus comes at the end

examples.text: What the committee eventually decided was to postpone the trip.
examples.note: the focus can be a to-infinitive

examples.text: What Nadia can't stand is being interrupted mid-sentence.
examples.note: the focus can be a gerund

use.point: Fixed clefts with reason, place and all

examples.text: The reason the museum closed early was a scheduled power cut.
The place where I feel most at ease is the school library.
All she asked for was a little more time.
examples.note: all-cleft, close in meaning to a wh-cleft

examples.text: That's why I double-check every source before I quote it.
examples.note: refers back to a reason just given

examples.text: That's what I've been trying to explain all along.
examples.note: refers back to an idea already mentioned

watch_out.wrong: Was Liam who found the mistake.
watch_out.right: It was Liam who found the mistake.
watch_out.why: An it-cleft must always start with it; it can never be dropped.

watch_out.wrong: It was the message what mattered.
watch_out.why: The connector after the focus is that (or who/which), never what.

watch_out.wrong: What worries me it is the silence.
watch_out.why: No extra subject pronoun after the wh-clause — the clause itself is the subject.

watch_out.wrong: The reason why the trip was cancelled was because of the weather.
watch_out.right: The reason the trip was cancelled was the weather.
watch_out.why: Choose either reason … why or because, not both — the two are redundant together.
A reversed wh-cleft needs what / why / how to introduce the clause, not that.

watch_out.wrong: All what she wanted was quiet.
watch_out.why: No relative pronoun after all in this pattern — the clause follows directly.

dialogue.title: Who really won the debate
dialogue.context: Nadia, Liam and Miss Vega go over Saturday's inter-school debate, correcting each other about what actually made the difference.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: So, be honest — what do you think decided the debate on Saturday?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: It was our rebuttal that swung it, not the opening statement.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: I disagree. What really impressed the judges was Sofia's closing argument.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Maybe, but it wasn't the argument itself that convinced them — it was how calmly she delivered it.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Interesting distinction. And the other team — why do you think they lost?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: The reason they struggled was a lack of evidence, not a lack of confidence.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Exactly. All they had was strong opinions, no statistics to back them up.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Fair point. What surprised you most about your own performance?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: What surprised me was how nervous I still felt, even after all that practice.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: That's exactly what I felt too — the nerves never really go away.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good. Now, one sentence each: what's the one thing you'll change for the next debate?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: The only thing I'll change is my timing — I ran over by a whole minute.

items.sentence: ___ Sofia who wrote the final paragraph, not Mateo.
items.why: An it-cleft for a specific past fact uses it was, matching the past tense of the story.

items.sentence: It was the noise ___ woke everyone up.
items.why: After an it-cleft focusing on a thing, the connector is that (or which), never what.

items.sentence: ___ annoys me most is people who don't listen.
items.why: A wh-cleft opens with what, not it or that.

items.sentence: ___ she wanted was a little peace and quiet.
items.why: All-cleft: All + clause + be + focus, with no extra relative pronoun.

items.sentence: ___ the concert was cancelled was a problem with the sound system.
items.why: Reason-cleft: The reason + clause + be + focus, not why or because, which would duplicate the idea.

items.sentence: I know it sounds strange, but ___ I meant.
items.why: A reversed wh-cleft is That's what + clause, referring back to something already said.

items.sentence: ___ we decided in the end was to reschedule the trip.
items.why: The focus of a wh-cleft can be a to-infinitive: What we decided was to reschedule.

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with one word so that it is grammatically correct.

items.sentence: ___ was the lighting, not the sound, that ruined the recording.
It was the lighting, not the sound, ___ ruined the recording.
___ surprised everyone was how quickly she answered.
___ she needed was a moment to think.
___ reason the flight was delayed was the storm.
That's ___ I've been saying all along.
___ only thing that matters now is the final score.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between two and five words.

items.first: The teacher's calm explanation reassured the class, not the extra handout.
items.second_end: the teacher's calm explanation that reassured the class, not the extra handout.

items.first: I can't stand people who arrive late without apologising.
items.second_end: people who arrive late without apologising.

items.first: She wanted nothing more than a little recognition.
The museum closed early because of a scheduled power cut.
items.second_end: the museum closed early was a scheduled power cut.

items.first: For that reason, I always check my sources twice.
items.second_end: I always check my sources twice.

items.first: The cost put them off, not the distance.
items.second_end: the distance that put them off; it was the cost.

summary: It-clefts (It was … that…) single out one element of a sentence, often to correct or emphasise a fact.
Wh-clefts (What … is…) build up to the important information, saving it for the end.
Fixed clefts with the reason / the place / the only thing / all follow the same clause + be + focus pattern.
Reversed wh-clefts (That's what/why/how…) refer back to something already said, especially in speech.
Overusing clefts sounds unnatural — save them for the one point you really want to stand out.
